derived_claims: This scatter plot, produced by Our World in Data, illustrates the relationship between global biomass (measured in tonnes of carbon) and the abundance (total number of individual organisms) of various taxonomic groups.
The data is based on a landmark 2018 study by Bar-On, Phillips, and Milo titled 'The biomass distribution on Earth'.
Because the values span many orders of magnitude—from billions to septillions in abundance, and millions to hundreds of billions in biomass—both axes are plotted on logarithmic scales.
Plants dominate global biomass, holding approximately 450 billion tonnes of carbon, despite having a relatively low abundance of around 100 billion individuals.

Microscopic organisms like Bacteria, Archaea, Protists, and Viruses exhibit astronomical abundances (ranging from hundreds of septillions to over one million septillion) and represent a massive share of global biomass, with Bacteria alone accounting for nearly 100 billion tonnes of carbon.
Animals, including humans, wild birds, and fish, represent a very small fraction of both global biomass and abundance compared to plants and microbes.

Humans are positioned near the bottom-left of the chart, with an abundance of around 10 billion and a biomass of roughly 60 million tonnes of carbon, while wild birds occupy the absolute lowest biomass position on the chart.
speculative_claims: In ecological studies, measuring biomass in tonnes of carbon (t C) is a standard method to compare the dry organic mass of different life forms, eliminating the variability of water weight across species.

This data challenges human-centric perspectives of life on Earth by demonstrating that humans and other familiar animal species make up a negligible fraction of the biosphere's total mass and population.

Understanding the distribution of biomass is critical for carbon cycle modeling, climate change mitigation strategies, and conservation biology, as plants and microbes perform the vast majority of global carbon sequestration and nutrient cycling.
If plant biomass continues to decline due to deforestation and land-use change, it could severely disrupt the global carbon balance.
